title: The Flatterer's Grand Feast of Words (MR)
summary: A parasitic courtier promises lavish feasts to guests but never serves food. Birbal invites him to a grand royal dinner of invisible delicacies.
full_text:
A boastful courtier named Mirza Kamran was famous in Agra for inviting poor scholars and poets to his mansion, describing magnificent menus of roasted lamb, saffron pilaf, and almond halwa, yet serving only dry water and stale crusts, saying: 'Imagine the heavenly flavor, my friends!'

The hungry poets complained to Birbal about the courtier's cruel teasing.

Birbal invited Mirza Kamran to a private royal banquet in the imperial pavilion, with Emperor Akbar observing behind a carved marble screen.

Kamran arrived in his finest silk robe, starving himself all day in anticipation.

Birbal seated the courtier before an empty gold platter and said with grand gestures:

'Welcome, noble Mirza! Let us begin our feast! Do you see this magnificent, imaginary soup of mountain pheasant and wild saffron? Smell the heavenly aroma! Take your golden spoon and drink deeply!'

Kamran was bewildered, but eager to please the powerful minister, he picked up his empty spoon, dipped it into empty air, and swallowed: 'Ah... delicious, Raja Birbal!'

Birbal continued enthusiastically: 'And now, behold this giant roasted royal peacock, stuffed with pistachios and raisins! Take this carving knife, slice off a fat drumstick, and chew the tender meat!'

The hungry courtier chewed empty air, his stomach rumbling loudly: 'Mmm... succulent... exquisite!'

Birbal then 'served' twenty imaginary courses—kababs, biryanis, sherbets, and pastries—making the courtier pantomime eating for two grueling hours!

Finally, Birbal smiled: 'And now, noble Mirza, since you have enjoyed the finest feast in Hindustan, let us have the palace wrestlers wrestle you in the courtyard to test your digestive strength!'

Mirza Kamran collapsed upon the floor, clutching his starving stomach, weeping: 'Mercy, Lord Birbal! I am dying of real hunger! I have swallowed only empty air!'

Akbar stepped out from behind the screen, laughing heartily:

'Now you know how those poor poets felt when you fed them grand words instead of real bread, Kamran! Words can comfort the soul, but they can never fill a hungry belly!'

Akbar ordered real food brought for the humbled noble, who swore never to mock the hungry again.
